owner: Built from the owner's own visitors and guests, so it's the warmest audience they have.

gloss: A rule that turns a URL or event detail into a conversion Meta can count and optimise for.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: We set up a custom conversion for the thank-you page so completed bookings get counted.
owner: Makes sure completed bookings get counted, so the owner's campaigns are judged on the right result.

gloss: Spend capped per day versus a fixed total spread across the schedule.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Is this on a daily or lifetime budget? It changes how we read the spend.
owner: Changes how spend lands over the schedule, which matters when comparing it with what the owner agreed to.

gloss: A client account marked Not Live or Paused that is still spending — the most important catch in HGM's ad spend check.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: This account is paused in our records but still spending — that's a dark account.
owner: An owner paying for ads on an account they think is paused is money spent without agreement, which is why it's the first thing HGM's check catches.

gloss: Meta's current name for a pixel together with its server connection and any other event sources; see Pixel.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026); Meta for Developers, Dataset Quality API (the dataset ID is the pixel ID), checked 29 Sep 2026.
usage: Meta now calls it a dataset, but it's the same pixel plus its server connection.
owner: If the owner sees 'dataset' in Meta, it's their pixel and server connection under a new name, not a new thing to pay for or set up.

gloss: The section of HGM's Benchmarks doc that is the only source of a campaign's state.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The Decision Making table sets a campaign's state, so check it before calling one weak.
owner: Keeps campaign calls consistent: every owner's campaign is judged against the same written rules.

gloss: Whether a campaign is active or paused, and whether an active one is actually serving — it can be active and still not deliver, for example past its stop time or stuck in learning limited.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The delivery status says active, but nothing's spending — let's check whether it's stuck in learning.
owner: A campaign can look active and still not be reaching anyone, so status alone doesn't tell the owner their money is working.

gloss: The metrics that explain a campaign's state but never set it — CPC, CPM, CTR, frequency and cost per booking.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Frequency and CPM are diagnostics — they explain why a campaign is struggling, but they don't decide its state.
owner: Explain why a campaign is doing what it's doing, so the fix addresses the cause rather than the symptom.

gloss: How HGM's weekly reports mark each issue against the week before, with the weeks it has been open counted.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: That issue has been still open for three weeks, so it needs an owner.
owner: Shows whether issues on the owner's account are being fixed or lingering week to week.

gloss: Revenue from direct bookings as recorded in the property's PMS.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Direct booking revenue comes from the PMS, not from Meta, so it's the owner's real number.
owner: The owner's own record of what direct bookings earned, which beats any platform's estimate.

gloss: The budget recorded in HGM's Master Meta Ads sheet against what the ad account is actually running.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The documented budget and the live budget don't match — the account is spending more than agreed.
owner: Checks that the owner is spending what they agreed to, no more and no less.

gloss: Meta combining the images, video and text you supply into variations and serving the best performers; since 2026 this is largely handled inside Advantage+ creative.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026); Campaign Builder, 'Meta flexible ads removed' (29 Apr 2026), checked 29 Sep 2026. Meta's Business Help Centre can't be read by automated tools, so this is checked against trade press only.
usage: Dynamic creative is mixing our headlines and images to find the best combination.
owner: Lets Meta test combinations of the owner's images and words to find what books, with less manual testing.

gloss: Meta's score, out of 10, for how well the customer details sent with an event match to real Meta users.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026); Meta for Developers, Dataset Quality API ('a score (out of 10)'), checked 29 Sep 2026.
usage: The EMQ score is low, so Meta can't match many of these bookings to real people — worth fixing.
owner: A low score means Meta can't match many bookings to real people, so it optimises the owner's ads on weaker signal.

gloss: Top, middle and bottom of funnel — building awareness, warming interest, then converting; HGM campaign names carry the prefix.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: This is a ToF campaign, so judge it on reach, not bookings.
owner: Each stage has a different job, so judging a top-of-funnel campaign on bookings would make good awareness spend look like waste.

gloss: Aiming ads by location — a country, listed cities, or a radius around a point.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Let's tighten the geo targeting to cities within a three-hour drive.
owner: Puts the owner's ads in front of the places guests actually come from.

gloss: A landing page built in GoHighLevel, HGM's landing-page and CRM tool, whose sub-account tracking settings carry the pixel ID.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The GHL funnel was cloned from another client, so check it isn't carrying their pixel.
owner: The landing page where the owner's leads sign up; if its pixel settings are wrong, those leads go uncounted or land in someone else's data.

gloss: The one metric that sets a campaign's state in HGM's reports — CPL for Lead Gen, ROAS for Sales.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: For a Lead Gen campaign, CPL is the governing metric — the others just help explain it.
owner: Keeps the verdict on each campaign simple and consistent: one number decides, the rest explain.

gloss: The short bold line that sits below an ad's creative.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Keep the headline short and specific — it's what people read after the image.
owner: Often the first words guests read after the image, so it has to say why this stay.

gloss: HGM's top-of-funnel Instagram campaigns, reported as a spend line only and not scored.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The IG Discovery campaigns are for awareness, so we report their spend but don't score them.
owner: Builds the audience that later books; judging it on bookings would cut the top of the owner's funnel.

gloss: The drop in tracking data after Apple's App Tracking Transparency prompt (iOS 14.5, April 2021), and the reason pixel numbers undercount and need cross-checking against booking data.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026); Apple Developer News, App Tracking Transparency requirement (26 Apr 2021), checked 29 Sep 2026.
usage: Because of iOS signal loss, the pixel undercounts bookings, so we always check against the booking data.
owner: Why Meta undercounts some bookings, and why HGM always checks against the owner's own booking data.

gloss: HGM's middle-of-funnel campaign type on the leads objective, usually retargeting engagers, scored on CPL over 30 days.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026) — the 30-day CPL window is stated in Shawal's doc, checked 29 Sep 2026. The Benchmarks doc itself wasn't reachable.
usage: The Lead Gen campaign is warming up past engagers, so we judge it on cost per lead.
owner: Builds the owner's email list from people already interested, the start of bookings that don't pay commission.

gloss: The period after a launch or significant edit when Meta is still working out delivery and results are unstable; it usually needs about 50 optimisation events in the 7 days after launch or the edit to exit.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026); consistent across trade press, checked 29 Sep 2026. Meta's Business Help Centre can't be read by automated tools, so this is checked against trade press only.
usage: The campaign is still in its learning phase, so give it a few days before making changes.
owner: Results bounce around at first, so judging or changing a new campaign too early wastes the owner's spend.

gloss: The share of impressions that became a click through to the site; the all-clicks CTR also counts likes, expands and profile taps.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Link CTR only counts clicks to the website, so it's the better measure of real interest.
owner: The share of people who actually went to the owner's website after seeing the ad, the better measure of interest.
example: Illustrative month of Meta ads: 4,800 link clicks ÷ 600,000 impressions × 100 = 0.8%.

gloss: The link in a social profile, used as a route to attribute bookings without the pixel.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: We track bookings from the link-in-bio separately, because the pixel doesn't always see them.
owner: Catches bookings the pixel misses, so the owner sees more of what social actually brought in.

gloss: People Meta judges similar to a seed audience you supply.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: A lookalike audience built from past guests helps us find new people like them.
owner: Finds new people who resemble the owner's best guests.

gloss: What the next booking costs at the current spend level, rather than the average.
formula: Extra spend ÷ Extra bookings it brought
source: revenue-management.md §2 (Marginal CPB)
usage: Adding more budget raises the marginal CPB — the next booking costs more than the last one.
owner: The next booking costs more than the last, so adding budget has limits the average cost doesn't show.
example: Illustrative: budget raised by $3,000 a month brings 6 more bookings. $3,000 ÷ 6 = $500.

gloss: An ad account the Meta connector can't read, so the weekly Ads Manager export is used instead.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: This is an MCP-disabled account, so we'll use the weekly Ads Manager export instead.
owner: The owner's reporting continues as normal; it's read from a weekly export instead of live, so figures may lag a few days.

gloss: Meta's public, searchable archive of every active ad, useful for checking what competitors are running.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Let's check the Meta Ads Library to see what other resorts nearby are running.
owner: Shows what competitors are running, useful for the owner's positioning.

gloss: Bookings tied to Meta through link-in-bio, a promo code or a UTM rather than the pixel.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: These Meta-attributed bookings came through promo codes, not the pixel.
owner: Bookings the owner can trace to Meta without relying on the pixel.

gloss: A sales-objective campaign aimed at lookalikes, with no band of its own, scored on the retargeting ROAS bands.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The MoF lookalike sales campaign is scored against the retargeting ROAS bands.
owner: Reaches new people similar to past guests with a direct booking offer.

gloss: First-time leads against every Lead event, including leads from Instagram tags.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Total leads look high, but new leads are flat — most are people we already had.
owner: Shows whether the owner's list is growing or just hearing from the same people again.

gloss: The outcome Meta optimises delivery for, such as leads, sales, awareness or engagement.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The objective tells Meta what to optimise for, so pick sales if bookings are the goal.
owner: Tells Meta what to spend the owner's budget trying to get, so the wrong one buys the wrong result.

gloss: Meta spend as a share of booking revenue.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Meta spend as a percent of booking value lets the owner compare ad cost with what an OTA would take.
owner: Puts the owner's Meta spend in the same terms as an OTA commission.
example: Illustrative month of Meta ads: $6,000 Meta spend ÷ $36,000 booking revenue × 100 = 16.7%.

gloss: Another client's domain firing events into a pixel, usually from a cloned GHL funnel still carrying the old pixel ID.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: We found pixel cross-contamination — another client's site is firing into this pixel.
owner: Another business's data landing in the owner's pixel distorts their results until it's fixed.

gloss: ROAS as Meta's pixel reports it, from the revenue Meta attributes to ads.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Pixel ROAS is what Meta reports, so we always say which ROAS we mean.
owner: Meta's own estimate of the revenue its ads brought; usually higher than what the owner's books show.
example: Illustrative month of Meta ads: $48,000 purchase conversion value ÷ $6,000 spend = 8.

gloss: Where an ad appears — Feed, Stories, Reels, Audience Network; Advantage+ placements lets Meta choose.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Reels placements are doing well for this property, so let's give them more of the budget.
owner: Where the owner's ads appear; some suit the property's content far better than others.

gloss: The main body text that sits above an ad's creative.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The primary text should say why this stay is different in the first line.
owner: Where the owner's story gets told in words; the first line has to earn the rest.

gloss: The booking revenue Meta attributes to an ad through purchase events.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Purchase conversion value is the booking revenue Meta credits to the ads.
owner: Meta's estimate of booking revenue from the ads, not the owner's actual books.

gloss: The count of whatever outcome the campaign's objective is set to, such as leads or purchases.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: In Ads Manager, results means whatever the objective counts — leads here, not bookings.
owner: Only as useful as the outcome being counted; leads and bookings aren't the same result.

gloss: HGM's bottom-of-funnel campaign type on the sales objective, retargeting site visitors, scored on ROAS over 14 days.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026) — the 14-day ROAS window is stated in Shawal's doc, checked 29 Sep 2026. The Benchmarks doc itself wasn't reachable.
usage: The Sales / Retargeting campaign shows ads to people who've already visited the website, so we judge it on ROAS.
owner: Brings back people who already visited the owner's site, the closest ads get to a booking.

gloss: The lookback period HGM scores each campaign type over; accounts read from a CSV fallback use a 21-day provisional window.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026) — the 21-day CSV fallback window is stated in Shawal's doc, checked 29 Sep 2026. The Benchmarks doc itself wasn't reachable.
usage: This account is on the CSV fallback, so it's using a shorter scoring window for now.
owner: Judges each campaign over a fair stretch of time, so one good or bad week doesn't decide it.

gloss: The domain a pixel's events come from, checked against the domains expected for that client.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Check the sending host — events should only come from the client's own domains.
owner: Confirms the owner's pixel is only hearing from the owner's own sites.

gloss: The two routes events reach Meta — the browser through the pixel, the server through CAPI — matched by a shared event ID so one booking isn't counted twice.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: We're getting browser events but no server events, which means CAPI isn't connected yet.
owner: Having both keeps the owner's bookings counted once and counted reliably.

gloss: A pixel sending zero or very few events for a client who is live.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: That client is live but the pixel is silent — something is broken on the site.
owner: Something on the owner's site is broken and bookings aren't being seen.

gloss: The minimum spend a campaign needs in its window before HGM scores it; below it, its state reads Under gate.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The campaign hasn't cleared the spend gate yet, so don't read too much into its numbers.
owner: Stops a campaign being judged before it has spent enough to mean anything.

gloss: The four flags HGM's ad spend check raises, set by the gap between documented and live budget and by any spend on accounts marked Not Live or Paused.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The spend check raised a Critical flag on this account, so it needs a look.
owner: A quick signal of whether the owner's spend matches what was agreed.

gloss: One client running two live pixels, so the funnel is either divided between them or counted twice.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: This client has split pixels, so half the funnel is reporting to the wrong place.
owner: Splits or double-counts the owner's results, so reports can't be trusted until it's fixed.

gloss: Meta's predefined names for site actions — PageView, ViewContent, Lead, InitiateCheckout, Purchase and so on.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Make sure the Purchase standard event fires on the confirmation page, not the checkout page.
owner: Named steps a guest takes on the site; the Purchase event has to fire at the right moment for bookings to count.

gloss: Where guest data is held and segmented for marketing; Revinate, Cendyn.
usage: Which CRM tool holds your guest list? We could use it to invite past guests back.
owner: Where the owner's guest list lives, and the difference between a one-time guest and a relationship.

core.hgm: HGM's own CRM is GoHighLevel, which the Client FAQs describe as HGM's customised CRM used for clients free of charge; a property's own hotel CRM is a separate system to connect to or export from.
core.confusions: A hotel CRM (Revinate, Cendyn) holds guest records from the PMS; GoHighLevel is HGM's marketing CRM for leads and email.

gloss: Pre-arrival and in-stay messaging to the guest; Duve, and Whistle (now part of Cloudbeds).
source: Whistle's acquisition by Cloudbeds (June 2022): PhocusWire, checked 25 Sep 2026; GlobeNewswire release, checked 29 Sep 2026.
usage: Your guest messaging tool is a good place to offer upgrades before arrival.
owner: Keeps the guest experience personal as the property grows, and gives the owner a pre-arrival moment to sell extras.

core.hgm: Pre-arrival is where HGM places upsells and expectation-setting (the pre-arrival sequence).
core.confusions: Guest messaging is one-to-one during the stay window; email marketing is one-to-many.

term: Rate shopping and market intelligence tools
gloss: Watching comp-set rates automatically; Lighthouse, formerly OTA Insight.
source: Lighthouse, rebrand from OTA Insight (Nov 2023), checked 29 Sep 2026.
usage: A rate shopping tool would show you what the resorts around you are charging each night.
owner: Shows the owner what the market is charging each night, which is context rather than a pricing rule.

core.hgm: The doctrine treats comp-set data as 'a guardrail, never a driver' and runs only a manual quarterly check (revenue-management.md §13).
core.confusions: Rate shopping tools show competitors' prices; benchmarking tools (STR) show their performance.

gloss: PMS, channel manager, booking engine, dynamic pricing — what each does and which names sit where.
source: PMS, channel manager, booking engine and CRS documentation from RoomMaster, SiteMinder, Inntopia and HotelSystemsGuide, 19 Sep 2026
usage: Which PMS, channel manager and booking engine are you on? That tells us what we can connect to.
owner: Knowing which systems the owner runs tells you what HGM can connect to and where their data lives.

core.hgm: The doctrine needs PMS sync and booking-engine events feeding Meta CAPI before activation (revenue-management.md §3.1). The HGM Client Tech Stack Guide puts vendor names to each category.
core.confusions: The PMS runs the property; the channel manager pushes rates and availability to OTAs; the booking engine takes direct bookings on the owner's site. One vendor, such as Cloudbeds, can do all three.

gloss: Paid upgrades before and at arrival; Oaky (part of Plusgrade since 2025).
source: PR Newswire, Plusgrade acquires Oaky (Oct 2025), checked 29 Sep 2026.
usage: An upsell tool can offer a room upgrade automatically a few days before check-in.
owner: Adds revenue per stay automatically, without staff having to sell.

core.hgm: Pairs with HGM's pre-arrival sequence; the doctrine keeps ancillary revenue management itself out of scope for v1 (revenue-management.md §13).
core.confusions: An upsell tool sells paid upgrades; a guest messaging tool handles conversation. Some platforms do both.

gloss: Booking.com, Expedia, Airbnb, Vrbo, plus Hipcamp, Glamping Hub, Mr & Mrs Smith.
source: Mr & Mrs Smith has been owned by Hyatt since June 2023 (LoyaltyLobby), checked 29 Sep 2026.
usage: Which OTAs and niche marketplaces are you listed on — just the big ones, or glamping sites too?
owner: Each listing brings visibility and a commission; niche marketplaces can reach guests the big OTAs don't.

gloss: Where the P&L is actually assembled.
usage: Your accounting system is where the real P&L lives, so that's where the final numbers come from.
owner: Where the owner's real P&L lives, and the final word on the numbers.

gloss: Scheduling and payment for tours, rentals and on-property experiences.
usage: If guests book tours through an activity booking system, we can promote those experiences too.
owner: If experiences can be booked online, they can be marketed and sold ahead of the stay.

gloss: The weekly CSV of campaign and ad set spend, budgets, purchases and leads, used where the connector can't read an account.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Pull the Ads Manager export for that account, since the connector can't read it.
owner: A fallback that keeps the owner's reporting going when a live connection isn't possible.

gloss: Comp-set performance reporting; STR (part of CoStar) for hotels, KeyData for vacation and short-term rentals.
source: CoStar STR Benchmark and keydata.co, checked 29 Sep 2026. No outdoor-hospitality benchmark was found.
usage: A benchmarking tool would show how you compare with similar properties nearby.
owner: Shows how the owner's performance compares with similar properties, if they subscribe to one.

gloss: HGM's Google Doc of campaign benchmarks, holding the Decision Making table.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The Benchmarks doc sets what good looks like for each campaign type.
owner: Sets what good looks like for each campaign type, so every owner's results are judged the same way.

gloss: Newbook, Campspot — the world a glamping client's stack usually comes from.
usage: Glamping clients often run on campground systems, which work differently from hotel software.
owner: Glamping owners often run on campground software, which changes what HGM can connect to.

gloss: HGM's Google Sheet of client booking revenue, the source for blended ROAS.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Blended ROAS comes from the Client Performance Tracking sheet, not from Meta.
owner: Holds the owner's booking revenue, the basis for the ROAS they can trust.

gloss: HGM's Google Sheet of client records, including whether each has a Basic or Advanced Meta setup.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Check the CRM sheet to see whether this client has a Basic or Advanced setup.
owner: Keeps each owner's setup on record, so whoever picks up the account knows what's been built.

gloss: Price comparison and nudges on the property's own site; Triptease, The Hotels Network.
usage: A direct-booking conversion tool shows guests they're getting the best price on your own site.
owner: Helps turn visitors on the owner's own site into direct bookings instead of OTA ones.

gloss: The tool a campaign is handed to when it reaches a Review or Scale state.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: Once a campaign reaches Review, it's handed to HG AI for a closer look.
owner: Where a campaign goes for a closer look when it's ready to review or scale.

gloss: GoHighLevel, ManyChat, Meta pixel and CAPI — what HGM connects into the above.
usage: Our own stack is what plugs into your booking tools, so it helps to know which pieces we use.
owner: The pieces HGM plugs into the owner's systems, so it's useful to know what connects where.

gloss: HGM's Google Sheet recording each client's documented Meta budget and status.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The Master Meta Ads sheet holds the agreed budget, so that's what we check the live spend against.
owner: Holds the budget the owner agreed to, which live spend is checked against.

gloss: The claude.ai connection that reads Meta ad accounts, campaigns and datasets live.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The Meta connector reads the ad accounts live, so the weekly check is up to date.
owner: Lets HGM read the owner's ad accounts live, so weekly checks are current.

gloss: The auto-generated meeting notes attached to HGM's Strategy and Sync calendar events.
source: Shawal Nazir, Meta Ads Terms (Google Doc, last edited 23 Sep 2026)
usage: The action items are in the Notes by Gemini from Tuesday's sync.
owner: Means decisions made about an owner's account on a call are written down and can be found later.

gloss: Card capture and processing inside the PMS.
usage: If payments are handled inside your PMS, deposits can be taken the moment someone books.
owner: Taking deposits at booking protects the owner from no-shows.

gloss: Review aggregation and response; Revinate, TrustYou.
usage: A reputation tool pulls all your reviews into one place so nothing goes unanswered.
owner: Keeps every review in one place so none goes unanswered.

gloss: Scheduling and payment for treatments; Book4Time, Mindbody.
usage: If spa treatments can be booked online, we can promote them in the pre-arrival email.
owner: Online spa booking makes treatments easy to sell before arrival.

gloss: The value of the best option you gave up by choosing another. In hospitality, it's usually the revenue a room, date or budget could have earned if it had been used differently.
usage: Holding that weekend for a possible wedding has an opportunity cost — the guests you turn away in the meantime.
owner: Every choice about a room, a date or a budget gives something else up; naming it helps the owner make the trade on purpose.

gloss: The mindset HGM's ICP is defined against.
usage: You're not an asset manager looking at a spreadsheet — you built this place, and that changes how we talk about it.
owner: HGM's ICP is the founder who cares about the place, not just the spreadsheet, which changes how every number should be framed.

gloss: NOI multiple, resort equity value, portfolio expansion — why NOI matters emotionally.
usage: Even if you never sell, knowing the exit vocabulary helps you see why growing NOI matters.
owner: Even owners who never plan to sell care what the business is worth; NOI and multiples are how that's measured.

gloss: Someone whose dream was to build this stay, who cares about the place and not just the spreadsheet.
usage: As an owner-operator founder, you care about the place as much as the numbers, and our marketing should reflect that.
owner: Their dream was to build this stay; icp.md says they 'care about the place, not just the spreadsheet', so lead with the place and bring the numbers in support.
